stations.name: Buchanan Street
stations.summary: The Subway's busiest station sits under pedestrianised Buchanan Street, with a moving walkway to Queen Street railway station. Built with one island platform, it gained a side platform in the 1977-80 rebuild.
stations.description:
Buchanan Street serves the city's main shopping thoroughfare and is the busiest station on the Subway (2.48 million passengers recorded in 2024). It opened with the line on 14 December 1896 with a single island platform serving both tracks.

The 1977-80 modernisation added a side platform. A glass wall now separates the island platform from the train boarding at the side platform, and each platform has a single stairway up to the ticket hall, which causes congestion in the peaks. Together with St Enoch it is one of only two stations with an underground ticket hall. The original street building on the east side of Buchanan Street was demolished to make way for the travelator to Queen Street mainline station; the remains of the old stairwell now serve as the entrance to the ticket hall at the end of that passage.

When Buchanan Street was pedestrianised in 1977, two new entrances were built in the middle of the former roadway, the northern one with escalators and the southern with a staircase. Both canopies were replaced in 1999; the northern canopy is made entirely of structural glass. The station was closed during the 2002 Glasgow floods, with trains passing through without stopping.
facts: Busiest station on the Subway: 2.48 million passengers in 2024.
A moving walkway links the ticket hall to Queen Street station, the only 'direct' Subway-mainline link apart from Partick.
The northern street canopy is built entirely of structural glass (beams, columns, walls and roof).
In 2002 floods closed the station while trains kept running through it.
Mainline Buchanan Street station (closed 1967) was over 500 m away and never connected to the Subway.
stations.architecture: Underground ticket hall with two pedestrian-street entrance canopies (1977, reglazed 1999); island platform plus added side platform separated by a glass screen; the old east-side surface building is gone.

stations.name: St Enoch

entrances.name: St Enoch Square station building (James Miller, 1896)

interchange: National Rail: Glasgow Central and Argyle Street (short walk)
stations.summary: Home of the Subway's most distinctive building: James Miller's red-sandstone Flemish-Renaissance station of 1896, now Category A listed and a coffee shop. The station below was rebuilt from scratch in the late 1970s and is the deepest in the city centre.
stations.description:
The surface building at St Enoch Square was designed by James Miller in 1896 in ornate Flemish Renaissance style in red sandstone. It housed the booking office and, upstairs, the headquarters of the Glasgow District Subway Company. It is Category A listed.

St Enoch is one of only two stations (with Partick) completely rebuilt from scratch in the 1977-80 modernisation. Because the listed building could not be demolished, its foundations were removed and a concrete box was built beneath it for the enlarged station and underground ticket hall; the building sat for a time on a precast platform above an empty void, then on the new station's concrete pillars. It was a travel information centre until 2008 and became a Caffe Nero in 2009.

St Enoch is the only station needing two escalator rides to reach the platforms because of its depth, and (with Govan) one of two that is wheelchair accessible. The modernised station has side platforms. The station is roughly halfway between Glasgow Central and Argyle Street railway stations and is the last station before the Subway dives under the River Clyde on the outer circle.
facts: Designed by James Miller (1896); the building also held the company's offices.
The listed station building was jacked onto a precast platform in the 1970s while the station below was rebuilt.
The only station needing two escalator rides to reach the platforms.
Its upper rooms were the headquarters of the Glasgow District Subway Company.
Next to the Clyde crossing: trains dive at roughly 1 in 18-20 beneath the river toward Bridge Street.
stations.architecture: Red sandstone Flemish Renaissance building (James Miller, 1896, Category A); concrete box station beneath it with underground ticket hall; side platforms.

stations.name: Bridge Street

entrances.name: Bridge Street station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: The first station south of the Clyde, serving Laurieston, Tradeston and the western Gorbals. It keeps its original island platform and is the main Subway-bus interchange for the south side.
stations.description:
Bridge Street station is at 67 Eglinton Street and serves Laurieston, Tradeston and the western fringe of the Gorbals. It opened on 14 December 1896 and was comprehensively modernised in 1977-80 while keeping the original island platform layout.

For a short time after opening it was an interchange with the adjacent Bridge Street railway station on the Glasgow and Paisley Joint Railway, which closed in the early 1900s. Today it is the main interchange between the Subway and buses to and from the south side. One of the system's five traction sub-stations stands at Bridge Street.

The tunnel between St Enoch and here is one of two Clyde crossings; it was driven under compressed air and was among the steepest on the line.
facts: Short-lived interchange with Bridge Street railway station (Glasgow & Paisley Joint Railway).
Houses one of the five Subway traction sub-stations.
About 378,000 gate entries a year in 2018-19.
stations.architecture: 1980 rebuild; island platform; compact street-level entrance on Eglinton Street.

stations.name: West Street

entrances.name: West Street station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: The quietest station on the network, in the Tradeston industrial area. Its steam cable-haulage engine house once stood between here and Shields Road.
stations.description:
West Street (281 West Street, Tradeston) serves Tradeston and Kingston and has been the least used station on the Subway, with under 100,000 boardings a year by 2012. Post-war reconstruction left it in an isolated industrial area; it was one of the original Park and Ride stations until its car park closed on 16 February 2008 for the M74 enabling works.

The station keeps its original island platform. The 1896 steam power station that drove the endless cables stood between West Street and Shields Road. It would become a major interchange if the proposed Glasgow Crossrail were built, and the Clyde Metro proposals also note a possible new West Street rail station.
facts: Least busy Subway station: 96,593 per SPT 2013-14 figures (104,709 in 2019).
The 1896 cable power station was sited between West Street and Shields Road.
Mentioned in Cliff Hanley's 'The Glasgow Underground'.

stations.name: Shields Road

entrances.name: Shields Road station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: Actually on Scotland Street, not Shields Road. Beside the M8, with a large Park and Ride and Mackintosh's Scotland Street School Museum nearby.
stations.description:
Shields Road station (30 Cornwall Street, Kingston) is actually on Scotland Street, and renaming has been considered. It serves Pollokshields and Kingston from an industrial area cut off by the M8 and the Kingston Bridge approach roads.

A Park and Ride car park with 839 spaces (rebuilt to over 800 spaces, finished September 2006) generates most of its trips. The Subway tunnels run directly beneath Scotland Street. The 1896 cable winding plant was close by on the line between here and West Street.

Nearby is Charles Rennie Mackintosh's Scotland Street School Museum.
facts: On Scotland Street, not Shields Road.
Park and Ride with 839 spaces.
About 511,000 entries in 2019.
stations.architecture: Island platform; 1980 station building with attached Park and Ride.

stations.name: Kinning Park

entrances.name: Kinning Park station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: The shallowest station on the system, beside the M8 near Plantation Park. The line is barely 7 ft below the surface hereabouts - the shallowest point of the whole circle lies between here and Cessnock.
stations.description:
Kinning Park serves the Kinning Park Industrial Estate and Plantation Park, with the M8 motorway alongside; a footbridge across the M8 has long been planned. It is the shallowest station on the Subway.

Historical sources put the shallowest point of the whole circle at about 7 ft (2.1 m) below the surface between Kinning Park and Cessnock, where the tunnels were built cut-and-cover. One of the five traction sub-stations (Cornwall Street) is on this stretch.

The station keeps its original island platform; new ticket barriers arrived on 10 July 2013.
facts: Shallowest station on the Subway.
Shallowest point of the circle: ~7 ft below surface, between Kinning Park and Cessnock.
Cornwall Street traction sub-station is near here.

stations.name: Cessnock
stations.summary: Entered through the basement of a tenement by Alexander 'Greek' Thomson, with no escalators and the Subway's last pre-modernisation livery and signage. Two iron arches mark the steps down.
stations.description:
Cessnock serves the eastern part of Ibrox and the Cessnock area, and is the nearest station to Festival Park and the Glasgow Science Centre/BBC Scotland campus. The entrance is at the east end of Walmer Crescent and passes under residential housing: you descend steps from a tenement basement, just below street level.

With Kelvinhall, it kept its pre-modernisation surface entrance, and it is the only station to retain its pre-modernisation livery and signage. In 1989, during restoration of the adjoining Alexander Thomson building, two metal arches bearing the station name were added over the steps; plans to remove them in a later refurbishment were dropped after public opposition.

There are no escalators; the island platform is original.
facts: Entrance is in a tenement basement beside a building by Alexander 'Greek' Thomson.
Only station keeping its pre-modernisation livery and signage.
Public opposition saved the 1989 iron arches.
stations.architecture: Tenement-basement entrance with iron arches; stairs only; original-style island platform and retained signage.

stations.name: Ibrox

entrances.name: Ibrox station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: Rangers' station: Copland Road until 1977, with an extra Woodville Street entrance opened on match days. Rebuilt with side platforms; upgraded 2014.
stations.description:
Ibrox opened as Copland Road and took its present name in 1977. It serves Ibrox and the home of Rangers F.C. Ibrox Stadium is close by. Surface buildings were replaced during the modernisation and the platform layout is described as side platforms (earlier island). A further upgrade opened in January 2014.

On match days the station is extremely busy; the main entrance remains on Copland Road and an additional entrance on Woodville Street opens to absorb the crowd. Otherwise it is quiet, with around half a million boardings a year (1.1 million in 2018).

The Broomloan depot connection leaves the running tunnels between Ibrox and Govan.
facts: Named Copland Road until 1977.
Extra Woodville Street entrance opens on match days.
Broomloan depot connection is just west on the way to Govan.
stations.architecture: Post-1980 surface building; side platforms; upgraded 2014.
stations.disputedPlatformLayout: Wikipedia station page says side platforms; the Subway page and others list an island layout. Treated as side.

stations.name: Govan
stations.summary: Govan Cross until 1977 and home of the Subway's depot. Rebuilt with side platforms after cracks in the roof closed the system early in 1977; step-free, with a lift and escalator.
stations.description:
Govan (737 Govan Road) opened as Govan Cross. In March 1977 cracks appeared in the station roof, suspending service until 2 May, and further cracking brought the final closure of the old Subway forward by eight days to 21 May 1977. The rebuilt station replaced the single island platform with two side platforms and reopened on 16 April 1980.

It has a lift and escalator, step-free access, and is one of two wheelchair-accessible stations (with St Enoch). It adjoins Govan bus station (six stands), and the Subway link to Partick is the only rail link across the Clyde west of the city centre, making it one of the busiest stations.

Just south lies Broomloan Depot, the only part of the system above ground, where the original cable-era workshops stood; trains were once lifted by crane onto the rails.
facts: Opened as Govan Cross; renamed Govan in 1980.
Roof cracks in March 1977 forced the closure of the whole system.
Only part of the Subway above ground, Broomloan Depot, is just to the south.
Subway link to Partick is the only rail crossing of the Clyde west of the city centre.
stations.architecture: 1980 station with side platforms, lift and escalator; Govan bus station adjacent.

stations.name: Partick
interchange: National Rail: Partick (North Clyde and Argyle lines)
stations.summary: The only Subway station with a direct National Rail interchange. Opened in 1980 to replace Merkland Street, with the bus station sandwiched between the Subway below and the railway above.
stations.description:
Partick station opened on 16 April 1980, replacing Merkland Street station some 25 m to the south-west, which closed with the old Subway on 21 May 1977. It was one of two stations built entirely from scratch in the modernisation and is the only Subway station connected directly to a National Rail station (North Clyde and Argyle lines).

At ground level is Partick bus station, above the Subway platforms and beneath the railway. The rail station was redeveloped from 2005 and reopened on 31 March 2009; the Subway platforms were renovated in 2012-13 for GBP 1.2 million. It has two side platforms, escalators but no lift (space for lifts has been safeguarded).

The Merkland Street 'ghost station' is still visible to drivers as a long straight, humped, large-diameter tunnel section.
facts: Only Subway station with a direct National Rail interchange.
Replaced Merkland Street, the system's only ghost station.
Bus station sits between the Subway below and the railway above.
stations.architecture: Late-1970s box station beneath the railway embankment; side platforms; escalators.

stations.name: Kelvinhall

entrances.name: Kelvinhall station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: Formerly Partick Cross. Entered from Dumbarton Road along a narrow arcade of shops below flats - one of two stations to keep its pre-modernisation entrance, with no escalators.
stations.description:
Kelvinhall (7 Dalcross Path) was called Partick Cross until 1977 and was renamed after the nearby Kelvin Hall; the unrelated Kelvin Hall railway station closed in 1964. The entrance is off Dumbarton Road, at the end of a narrow arcade of shops below flats, and is barely visible from the street without signage.

Renovation was less extensive than at most stations; with Cessnock it kept its original entrance and surface building, and it keeps its original island platform and has no escalators. It is one of two stations serving Kelvingrove Park and the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum area.
facts: Renamed from Partick Cross in 1977.
Entrance is an arcade of shops under flats - the last 'shopfront' Subway entrance.
No escalators.
stations.architecture: Retained pre-modernisation shopfront entrance and stair; original island platform.

stations.name: Hillhead
stations.summary: The West End's station on Byres Road: first to be modernised (2011-12), with an Alasdair Gray ceramic mural. Deep under the hill, with an island and a side platform.
stations.description:
Hillhead is the principal Subway station serving the West End, on Byres Road, near the University of Glasgow and Botanic Gardens, with 1.86 million boardings a year.

Originally a single island platform, it gained an additional side platform and a larger ticket office with escalators in 1977-80. It was the first station in SPT's modernisation: a GBP 1.5 million refit with new escalators, tiling, wayfinding and a new ticket office finished in 2012. Alasdair Gray and Nichol Wheatley's ceramic mural of the surrounding district was unveiled on 16 September 2012.

The tunnels around Hillhead are the deepest of the circle: historical sources cite about 115 ft (35 m) here and some 155 ft (47 m) below Glasgow Street, near the Kelvin crossing. A traction sub-station (Byres Road) stands here.
facts: First station in SPT's 2010s modernisation (completed 2012).
Alasdair Gray ceramic mural, unveiled 16 September 2012.
Deepest tunnels of the circle are beneath Hillhead (about 35-47 m).
stations.architecture: Wide ticket hall with two escalators and a staircase; island platform plus side platform with a perspex barrier.

stations.name: Kelvinbridge

entrances.name: Kelvinbridge station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: The deepest station on the Subway, beside the River Kelvin; pumps run continuously against seepage. The 1980 rebuild reversed the entrance onto Great Western Road.
stations.description:
Kelvinbridge serves Woodlands, Woodside and Hillhead and is named after the bridge over the River Kelvin. It is the deepest station on the system because of its proximity to the river, and seepage means pumps run continuously. It is also the busiest station to keep its original island platform.

It was originally reached through a tenement block on South Woodside Road, with an external cast-iron staircase down from Kelvinbridge to Great Western Road. The 1977-80 rebuild reversed the entrance: a new surface ticket hall opened with its main entrance on Great Western Road, reached by a glass-enclosed escalator; the old entrance became an emergency exit. The car park sits on the former goods yard of Kelvinbridge railway station.

The tunnels cross the River Kelvin just west of the station.
facts: Deepest station on the Subway; constantly pumped.
Before 1977 it was the only station with a lift (withdrawn in the rebuild).
Park and Ride on the old Kelvinbridge railway goods yard.
stations.architecture: 1980 glass-enclosed escalator entrance on Great Western Road; old cast-iron stair retained as emergency exit.

stations.name: St George's Cross

entrances.name: St George's Cross station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: Its surface building was rebuilt in 1971 for the Inner Ring Road (M8), the only station rebuilt before the 1977-80 modernisation, then re-clad in the new corporate style.
stations.description:
St George's Cross serves Woodside and Woodlands and the eastern end of Great Western Road. It keeps its original island platform. The area around the Cross was reconfigured by the M8 Inner Ring Road, and the surface buildings were demolished and rebuilt in 1971; this concrete-aggregate-clad building was re-clad during modernisation in the dark brown brick and orange tiling of the new corporate style.

The junction itself has been realigned and carries far less traffic than before.
facts: Only station substantially rebuilt before the 1977-80 modernisation (1971).
About 544,000 boardings in 2011-12.
stations.architecture: Rebuilt 1971 in concrete aggregate, then re-clad in brown brick/orange tile (1980).

stations.name: Cowcaddens

entrances.name: Cowcaddens station building
entrances.source: approximate (OSM station node/building; no entrance node mapped)

stations.summary: The Garnethill station for the Glasgow School of Art area. By 1972 its entrance was the only building left standing after the Comprehensive Development Area demolitions.
stations.description:
Cowcaddens serves Cowcaddens, Garnethill and Dundasvale on the north side of the city centre. Its original entrance was part of a shop unit in a tenement. After the area was declared a Comprehensive Development Area in the 1960s and the surrounding buildings demolished, the station entrance was by 1972 the only structure left standing.

The 1977-80 rebuild added a new surface ticket hall and escalators but kept the original island platform. It was marginally the closest Subway stop to the old Buchanan Street railway station (closed 1967). The Dundasvale traction sub-station is here.
facts: By 1972 the entrance was the only building standing in the area.
Near the Glasgow School of Art, the Royal Conservatoire and Chinatown.
stations.architecture: 1980 ticket hall with escalators; original island platform.

outer.name: Outer Circle
outer.note: Last point is one spacing short of closing on the first (closed loop); s is metres along the direction of travel from the Buchanan Street platform centre.

inner.name: Inner Circle
inner.note: Last point is one spacing short of closing on the first (closed loop); s is metres along the direction of travel from the Buchanan Street platform centre.

tunnel.lining: cast iron segmental rings (British Hydraulic Foundry, Whiteinch) or mass concrete; brick-lined in places; much cut-and-cover under streets; river crossings driven under compressed air
tunnel.construction: Engineers Simpson & Wilson; contractors incl. Robert McAlpine (rock), Charles Brand, Hugh Kennedy, John Patterson, George Talbot, David Shanks, Watt & Wilson, James Smith. Two parallel single-bore tunnels, each opening into a single 28 ft-span arch at island-platform stations.
tunnel.minRadiusNote: Sharpest curve reported as 660 ft radius (Cassier 1898); the supplied smoothed centreline has locally tighter apparent curvature in places.
tunnel.maxGradient: 1 in 18 (5.6%) and 1 in 20 (5%) beneath the Clyde (1898 report); stations sit at summits of ~1 in 40 so trains climb into and fall out of each platform

depthRangeM.minNote: 7 ft below surface between Kinning Park and Cessnock
depthRangeM.maxNote: 155 ft below Glasgow Street near Hillhead

tunnel.riverCrossingsNote: Clyde crossed twice (St Enoch-Bridge Street, Govan-Partick), Kelvin once (Hillhead-Kelvinbridge).

ghostStation.name: Merkland Street
ghostStation.note: Closed 21 May 1977; replaced by Partick (25 m NE). A long straight humped large-diameter tunnel section marks the site; no platforms remain.

depot.name: Broomloan Depot
depot.location: Govan, between Govan and Ibrox stations
depot.connection: Ramp/points off both tunnels between Ibrox and Govan (1977-80); before 1977 trains were craned onto the line at Govan workshops
depot.note: Only above-ground part of the system

riverCrossings.name: River Clyde (Glasgow Bridge reach, St Enoch to Bridge Street)

current.name: Stadler Subway train (third generation)
current.builder: Stadler Rail, Altenrhein (Switzerland); signalling Ansaldo STS (Hitachi Rail)
current.formation: articulated 4-car, open gangway; motor bogies on the two end cars (Bo'Bo'+2'+2'+Bo'Bo')
current.lengthNote: sources: 39.2-39.51 m (same overall length as the 3-car train it replaced)
current.accelNote: ESTIMATE - not published in sources found
current.operation: Designed for unattended (driverless) operation; platform screen doors + CBTC being installed through 2026; contract GBP 200 m (2016)

history.name: Cable-hauled gripper cars
history.builder: Oldbury Railway Carriage & Wagon (gripper cars, 1896-97); Hurst Nelson, Motherwell (trailers, 1898+)
history.note: Wooden bodies; lattice gates at ends; doors one side only; endless cable gripper; livery plum and cream; 20+10 gripper cars, 30 trailers

history.name: Electrified 1896 cars
history.supply: 600 V DC third rail with skids
history.note: Converted 1935 (GBP 120,000); red and white then all-red livery; air-operated doors in 1960s; "Shoogly Train"; withdrawn 1977; car 41 preserved

history.name: Metro-Cammell second generation
history.builder: Metro-Cammell, Washwood Heath (33 cars 1977-79; 8 centre trailers by Hunslet 1992); GEC motors; refurbished ABB Derby 1993-95
history.note: Bright orange livery ("Clockwork Orange"), later Strathclyde red then cream and carmine (2006) then orange (2011); automatic train operation with driver closing doors; withdrawn 28 June 2024

timeline.title: Authorised
timeline.text: The Glasgow District Subway Act 1890 authorises the Glasgow District Subway Company.

timeline.title: Construction begins
timeline.text: Tunnelling starts, a mixture of cut-and-cover, brick tunnelling and iron-lined bores; the Clyde is crossed under compressed air.

timeline.title: Opening day, 14 December
timeline.text: The cable-hauled circle opens with 15 stations. That night one car carrying 60 passengers is struck by another under the Clyde; four are injured and the line closes until 19 January 1897.

timeline.title: Municipal ownership
timeline.text: Glasgow Corporation takes over the company for GBP 385,000.

timeline.title: Electrification
timeline.text: Cars converted to 600 V DC third-rail power; the last cable-hauled service runs on 30 November 1935 (driver Robert Boyd). The system is renamed the Glasgow Underground in 1936.

timeline.title: Wartime bomb
timeline.text: On 18 September a German bomb lands on a bowling green south of Merkland Street and damages both tunnels; part of the line stays shut until January 1941.

timeline.title: St George's Cross rebuilt
timeline.text: The surface building is rebuilt for the Inner Ring Road.

timeline.title: Closure for modernisation
timeline.text: Cracks in the roof of Govan Cross bring closure on 21 May 1977, eight days early. Stations are rebuilt, side platforms added, Merkland Street closed and Partick planned.

timeline.title: Royal inauguration
timeline.text: On 1 November 1979 the Queen and Prince Philip ride from Buchanan Street to St Enoch.

timeline.title: Reopening, 16 April
timeline.text: The modernised Glasgow Underground opens with new orange Metro-Cammell trains, automatic train operation and new ticketing.

timeline.title: Fourth car added
timeline.text: Eight centre trailers make all trains three-car.

timeline.title: Back to "Subway"
timeline.text: SPT officially readopts the name Subway.

timeline.title: Hillhead refurbished
timeline.text: First station of the SPT programme completed; Alasdair Gray mural unveiled.

timeline.title: Stadler contract
timeline.text: SPT awards Stadler and Ansaldo STS a GBP 200 m contract for 17 driverless-capable trains.

timeline.title: New trains in service
timeline.text: First passenger service with Stadler trains on 11 December 2023.

timeline.title: Old trains retired
timeline.text: The Metro-Cammell fleet is withdrawn on 28 June 2024.

timeline.title: Contactless and screen doors
timeline.text: Contactless payment introduced; platform screen doors being commissioned station by station.
